## The question

An hour ago, describing a tangram likely took you a whole sentence. By round six, a couple of words did the same job, and your partner found the right picture *faster*. Somewhere in those rounds, the two of you built something: names for the shapes that only you two share, resting on everything you now both know about what worked before. That growing pool of shared knowledge is what yesterday's lecture called **common ground**, and the private names are **conventions**: agreements about what words mean.

Grice's idea from yesterday connects the two: speakers say as much as is needed, and no more. In round one, a lot is needed. Your partner knows nothing yet. By round six, almost nothing is needed, because the common ground carries most of the load. Fewer words, *more* understanding. *What is needed*, then, tends to shrink as common ground grows.

That's the story for two people. But what happens if you need to build common ground with a whole group at once? Describing for five listeners is a different job: they don't all know the same things, they can't all ask questions, and a name that clicks for one of them may mean nothing to the rest.

So today has two questions. 

- When two people talk about the same things again and again, what happens to the words they use? 
- What changes when the audience grows?

We'll use data from two published studies of exactly this game. In the first, 83 pairs played it over online chat, so every message they typed is preserved (Hawkins, Frank & Goodman, 2020). In the second, the same game was played by 104 groups of two to six people — one describer, the rest matching (Boyce, Hawkins, Goodman & Frank, 2024).

## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this seminar, you will be able to:

- Trace how referring expressions compress across repeated reference, in raw messages and in numbers.
- Show that pairs say *less* while understanding *more*, and explain why that isn't a paradox.
- Compare experimental conditions: what does audience size do to compression and to understanding?
- Match a measure to the right unit, and say why words-per-message and words-per-description can tell different stories.

## How it works

Same format as last week. Work with your partner from the game. Wherever you see `____`, you write the code; everything comes from the last two Fridays, plus exactly one new ggplot move, introduced when you need it.

Start with [Block 1 · The corpus](01_meet_the_data.qmd).

Hawkins, R. D., Frank, M. C., & Goodman, N. D. (2020). Characterizing the dynamics of learning in repeated reference games. Cognitive science, 44(6), e12845.

Boyce, V., Hawkins, R. D., Goodman, N. D., & Frank, M. C. (2024). Interaction structure constrains the emergence of conventions in group communication. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 121(28), e2403888121.
